body_markdown:
Formula 1 is returning to Africa after a decades-long hiatus. Rwanda will host the African Grand Prix for 10 years starting in the early 2030s, and the race will be held on a new track being designed and built near Rwanda’s capital specifically for the event.


Shown above in an official rendering, the new track is being designed with the help of Tilke Engineering and Wurz Designs. Tilke Engineering has designed major tracks around the world, including the Baku City Circuit, Kuwait Motor Town, and the Las Vegas Strip Circuit. Wurz Designs boasts a similar level of experience, and its team of designers includes Le Mans winner Alex Wurz.


The track will be located near Kigali, Rwanda’s capital, in a city called Bugesera. Wurz, who has worked on the project for several years, says the region’s topography is ideal for a track because it’s hilly and dotted with small lakes. While work is ongoing, the current plan is to build a 17-turn, 3.7-mile circuit with about 650 feet of elevation change per lap. The layout will also include cambered turns and banking, and races will run counterclockwise. Tilke describes the track as a roller coaster.


For context, the Strip Circuit that[the Las Vegas Grand Prix](https://www.hagerty.com/media/motorsports/las-vegas-f1-grand-prix-la-nouvelle-epoque-brings-hard-lessons/) is held on stretches about 3.8 miles and also has 17 turns. And the 650-foot elevation change is massive: Drivers deal with 334 feet of elevation change on the Belgian Grand Prix’s Spa circuit.


Wurz, Tilke, and other partners are busily testing potential track layouts on simulators. Their goal is to open the track in the early 2030s, though there’s no word on when the venue will host its first African Grand Prix. And it’s not just for Formula 1: The track is being designed to host “a wide range of motorsport disciplines.” It will notably include a karting facility and off-road courses.


The paddock buildings will feature typical Rwandan architecture, and the other buildings on-site will also be used for other, non-racing-related events such as concerts. Conveniently, the track will be close to the international airport scheduled to open in 2028.


Officials in Rwanda hope the publicity and investments generated by the upcoming African Grand Prix will benefit neighboring nations as well, which explains why it’s not called the “Rwanda Grand Prix” or the “Kigali Grand Prix.”


“For decades, African athletes have been a pillar of the global sports economy, adding significant commercial value to top leagues, with the continent receiving almost nothing in return. Partnerships like the one we are building help break this cycle,” explained Paul Kagame, the president of Rwanda, in a statement. His team’s goal is to turn Rwanda into a major tourist and sport destination.


Formula 1 said races usually generate over $130 million in annual economic impact in new host nations. It’s not just the spectators: Getting teams to a country, preparing for the race, and packing everything up injects a massive amount of money into an economy.


Rwanda will join Morocco and South Africa as the only African countries that Formula 1 has been to. Morocco held a race on the Ain-Daib road course in 1958, while South Africa held 23 races (notably on the Kyalami track) but fell off the calendar in 1993.
